query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable, protective oxide layer above 900 °C is controlled by the identity of the X element. When X is Si or Al, their high oxygen affinity and low oxygen diffusivity promote the preferential formation of coherent, slow-growing, adherent oxide films (SiO2 or Al2O3) that act as effective diffusion barriers. In contrast, when X is Mn, its rapid oxidation produces porous, non-coherent Mn-rich oxides that spall and deplete the alloy of Mn, leading to unstable coverage.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloys fabricated as single- or multiphase solid solutions with a homogeneous distribution of elements.
generation.intervention: Alter the alloy composition by substituting the X element; compare alloys with X = Si or Al against alloys with X = Mn.
generation.conditions: Exposure to oxidative or corrosive atmospheres at temperatures above 900 °C (e.g., 950 °C) for extended periods (e.g., 100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: Surface segregation and interfacial coherency between the oxide scale and the underlying alloy; the lattice mismatch and strain at the oxide/alloy interface.
generation.mechanism: Differential oxygen affinities and diffusivities of the X element govern oxide formation. Si and Al segregate to form dense, slow-growing oxide scales (SiO2 or Al2O3) that remain coherent with the substrate, whereas Mn oxidizes rapidly to form porous, unstable Mn-rich oxides. This difference in kinetics and interfacial bonding drives the stability of the protective layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Si or Al will develop a continuous and adherent oxide layer that remains intact during prolonged high-temperature exposure, while alloys with X = Mn will exhibit cracked, spalled, or non-protective oxide layers accompanied by compositional depletion from the bulk.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNiMn alloy, where Mn oxidation leads to the formation of unstable, porous oxides that spall under high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for exposures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive environments; oxide stability and formation mechanisms may differ at lower temperatures or in inert atmospheres.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative differences in oxide scale thickness, growth rate, and stress state between the different X substitutions are not fully established, and the influence of multiphase microstructure on diffusion kinetics may introduce variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of CrFeCoNiX HEA samples with identical processing history, varying only the X element (X = Si, Al, or Mn). Expose all samples in a controlled furnace environment at 950 °C under both oxidative and corrosive atmospheres for 100 hours. Pre- and post-exposure, use SEM, XRD, and EDS to assess the morphology, composition, thickness, and adherence of the oxide scales.
measurements: Continuity and uniformity of the oxide layer (via SEM imaging)
Phase identification of the oxides (using XRD)
Oxide composition and elemental distribution (using EDS)
Assessment of spallation or cracking (mechanical adhesion tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with X = Si or Al do not exhibit significantly more continuous, coherent, and adherent oxide layers than the Mn-containing alloy, or if the Mn alloy unexpectedly forms a protective oxide comparable to the Si/Al variants, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

Abstract Oxidation behavior of a refractory AlNbTiVZr 0.25 high-entropy alloy at 600–900 °C was investigated. At 600–700 °C, two-stage oxidation kinetics was found: Nearly parabolic oxidation (n = 0.46–0.48) at the first stage, transitioned to breakaway oxidation (n = 0.75–0.72) at the second stage. At 800 °C, the oxidation kinetics was nearly linear (n = 0.92) throughout the entire duration of testing. At 900 °C, the specimen disintegrated after 50 h of testing. The specific mass gains were estimated to be 7.2, 38.1, and 107.5, and 225.5 mg/cm 2 at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 100 h, and 900 °C for 50 h, respectively. Phase compositions and morphology of the oxide scales were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). It was shown that the surface layer at 600 °C consisted of the V 2 O 5 , VO 2 , TiO 2 , Nb 2 O 5 , and TiNb 2 O 7 oxides. Meanwhile, the scale at 900 °C comprised of complex TiNb 2 O 7 , AlNbO 4 , and Nb 2 Zr 6 O 17 oxides. The oxidation mechanisms operating at different temperatures were discussed and a comparison of oxidation characteristics with the other alloys was conducted. Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.
